analytic.title: An EtherCAT-based Motor Drive for High Precision Motion Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Industrial Ethernet-based motor drives offer many advantages for motion applications. This paper presents the implementation and analysis of a motor drive with the EtherCAT, an open real-time Ethernet standard, for high-precision motion systems. Considering the characteristics of the multitasked software and the network interface, we analyze the delay in actuating the motor in response to a command from the control host. Based on a response time analysis and the times measured from the developed drive, we discuss performance characteristics of the drive in respect of the end-to-end delay and the maximum achievable throughput for non-real-time traffic when the drive is controlled in position, velocity, or torque mode.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Precision motion systems refer to multi-motor systems with the ability of highly sychronized actuation and near-or belowmillisecond scale periodic control over the constituent motor drives. Being used in such mission-critical applications as medical operation, industrial automation, and military machinery, they inherently impose strict timing constraints on their behaviour. Typically, a cycle time less than 1 ms is needed. For this reason, aiming for improved responsiveness of the motor drives, many of precision motion systems have used dedicated analog links for the connection of the central motion controller and the drives. Analog link-based motion systems, however, have many drawbacks: analog links are susceptible to external noise, have low resolutions, and limit the scalability due to the complex and bulky analog cabling [19]. Recently, with the standardization of the real-time Ethernet for industrial applications [4], [5], Ethernet-based motion systems are gaining increasing interest [8], [16], [17], [11].

In motion systems, the real-time Ethernet offers many advantages over the analog links. Firstly, the high transmission speed of Ethernet significanlty reduces the cycle time, enabling a higher degree of motion precision which could not have been achieved with other digital fieldbuses. Secondly, the high availability of commercial off-the-shelf Ethernet hardware and software components can greatly contribute to the costcompetitiveness as the real-time Ethernet gets widely adopted. Thirdly, the globally synchronized clock available with many of the real-time Ethernet specifications makes possible the design of highly synchronized actuation over a large number Kanghee Kim is the corresponding author. For further information, please contact him at khkim@ssu.ac.kr. of motor drives. Finally, the compatibility with the higherlevel protocols, e.g., TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and IP (Internet Protocol) facilitate the administration and diagonostics operations using well-established application protocols such as HTTP and SNMP. This can expedite the integration of both the communication buses for management and process information, leading to a grealy simplified system architecture.

Notwithstanding the benefits of the Ethernet-based motion systems, however, there has been little work to accurately characterize the real-time Ethernet-based motor drives. For the design of precision motion systems with highly synchronized motor actuation, it is essential to analyze the responsiveness and throughput of the motor drives in a holistic way considering both the hardware and software layers involved, which include the control loop and upper-layer protcol stacks. Most of previous relevant work, however, only deals with either the implementation issues [14], [16], [17] or the analysis of the underlying communication buses [15], [18], [12], thus lacking a complete view on the motor drive behaviour.

In this paper, we address the implementation and analysis of an EtherCAT-based motor drive system with a multitasked software architecture. EtherCAT is a promising real-time Ethernet which is standardized in IEC 61158 and 61784 [4], [5]. When designing a networked motor drive system, the designer should be able to address important performance measures such as the response time for the actuation of a command issued by the control host and the maximum throughput for non-real-time data. With our drive software implmentation, the jobs for motor actuation and sensing and the jobs for data communication are handled by separate tasks. Considering the behavioural features of the communication link and the implemented software, we analyze the worst-case end-to-end delay for the command actuation. The achievable maximum throughput for non-real-time traffic is also investigated. Based on the analysis and experimental measurement, we discuss the performance characteristics of the drive according to the master control period and command mode: the position, velocity, and torque modes. Note that this paper is distinguished from our previous work [20] in that the former details the implementation of the drive system and gives a deterministic delay analysis while the latter focuses on a general methodology to determine a guaranteed precision of the motion system in the stochastic domain.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we describe the background to the EtherCAT and networked motion systems. Section III introduces the implementation of an EtherCAT-based motor drive with a standardized interface. Based on the developed drive, in Section IV, we analyze and discuss the performance. Section V summarizes the paper.

div.head: A. EtherCAT: a Real-time Ethernet Specification
div.p: EtherCAT is an open real-time Ethernet specification that is originally developed by Beckhoff [1]. It is now being increasingly adopted in various industrial and research fields. This section briefly introduces the EtherCAT focusing on its features relevant to precision motion systems. The EtherCAT offers high-speed deterministic packet transmission [11]. Fig. 1 shows the organization of a typical EtherCAT network consisting of one master and a number of slaves. In a bus topology, the master that is placed on either end can initiate the transmission of packet frames, in which every slave has a dedicated area for data communication and reads/writes its process data as the packets traverse the network. The packets, after reaching the end slave in the bus, eventually return to the master. Since packets are forwarded by a hardware switch inside every node and nodes are connected peer-to-peer, a time-deterministic communication is guaranteed among the participant nodes. Thanks to the short packet forwarding delay, usually less than 500 ns, the EtherCAT can achieve a cycle time of less than 1 ms for typical configuration [15]. Out of industrial applications, the motion system is known to have the most demanding requirement on the underlying network because it should be able to synchronize the actuation of a large number of motors. The low-jitter highspeed communication performance of the EtherCAT is very attractive for the design of such motion systems.

The EtherCAT also supports delivery of non-real-time traffic using the slack time left after conveying the real-time data. In EtherCAT, there exist two types of fundamental communication functions: the mailbox and process data services. The process data service is used for periodic real-time data and the mailbox service for aperiodic non-real-time data, e.g., IP packets. The support for IP packets over the mailbox can be effectively used for implementing remote administration of the motor drives.

With EtherCAT, the clocks of the distributed drives can be synchronized by means of the global clock called distributed clock. Global clock is essential for highly synchronized multimotor actuation. Using timestamped frames, the EtherCAT adjusts the local clock to compensate the propagation delay at each node. It is reported that the clock skew is far below 1 μs for common organization [10].

div.head: B. Motion Control Systems
div.p: As shown in Fig. 1, a networked motion system with industrial Ethernet is composed of a control host and a number of motor drives. The control host periodically sends control commands and coordinates the distributed motors for the desired motion. Each drive actuates its associated motors in accordance with the received command and sends the motor status back to the host. Note that all the control loops are kept in the drives. Compared with the conventional analog-linkbased motion systems where the control host typically embeds the major control loops thus having limited scalability due to the huge computational burden, the Ethernet-based system can accommodate greatly larger number of motor drives with a single control host.

The motor drive operates in one of three command modes: the position, velocity, and torque modes. Depending on the motion application, the control host determines which command mode to use during the initialization phase. As shown in Fig. 2, our EtherCAT-based drive hardware is mainly composed of a DSP, main memory, a flash ROM, an EtherCAT controller, and an ASIC. The DSP is responsible for running the control loops and upper-level network protocol stacks. Our drive uses a TI TMS320VC33 DSP with 60 MIPS [7]. The NAND flash memory is used for storing device-specific profiles for service configuration and process data. As the EtherCAT slave controller (ESC), the Beckhoff ET1100 chip is adopted [6]. The ESC handles the physical and link layer functions in hardware. By incorporating a dual-ported RAM (DPRAM), it facilitates the data copy between the controller and the DSP without any blocking. The

div.p: ASIC includes such dedicated functions as digital-to-analog conversion of the DSP-generated waveform, encoder pulse circuit, direction decoder, and sensor interface. A permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) is used in our system.

div.head: B. Multitasked Software for Control and Communication
div.p: The drive software has been developed in a multitasked structure using priority-based preemptive scheduling. Considering the resource-constrained drive environment, the kernel was carefully designed to minimize the overheads by including only basic primitives such as task scheduling, timer, and synchronization. Also the data structures and algorithms have been specifically optimized for the target DSP: for example, unused registers, R5 -R7, which were identified in code inspection were excluded from the task context and the scheduling primitives were rewritten to use efficient instructions based on barrel shifter.

Based on the above kernel primitives, the drive function has been decomposed into four tasks: the MotorAct, MotorMon, MsgInt, and MsgMain tasks. Table I summarizes the resulting tasks with their priorities and periods. Note that priorities are assigned according to the rate monotonic algorithm. giving the higher priority to the task with the shorter period [21].

The MotorAct task executes the control loop, generating a pulse-width-modulated (PCM) waveform to make the associated motor to reach the requested target position, velocity, or torque. For correct control of the motor, the MotorAct requires a high degree of periodicity in its execution -typically, a task jitter of more than a few microseconds is unacceptable. So, it has been assigned the highest priority. MotorAct is also responsible for updating the motor status information using the sensed data from the motor. The status information is later copied to the DPRAM in the ESC by the MsgInt task and ultimately fedback to the host.

The MotorMon task monitors the status of the motor and detects warning conditions such as overload and overcurrency. On the occurrence of such warning conditions, it may perform an emergency stop considering the severity and the consequence. The MotorAct and MotorMon tasks are released based on the kernel timer that is set to a period of 50 μs in our configuration. So, the task periods are restricted to a multiple of 50 μs. The periods for the MotorAct and MotorMon tasks have been determined by the requirements of the ASIC and motor hardware and set to 50 μs and 500 μs, respectively.

The MsgInt task handles the real-time process data in response to the interrupts from the ESC. A successful run of the MsgInt reads process output, e.g., the target position from the ESC into the main memory, and writes the process input, e.g., the actual position from the main memory to the ESC. These process data in the main memory are shared with the MotorAct and used for actuation and status update. The MsgInt can also be modeled as a periodic task with the period corresponding to the master cycle time, i.e., the period of commands issued by the control host. Our observation results confirm that the interrupts from the EtherCAT frame have a high degree of periodicity with a jitter of 2 -3 μs. In our analysis, we assume that the period of MsgInt is greater than 50 μs. In Section IV, we will discuss the minimum feasible period and its effect on the maximum achievable throughput for non-real-time data, which is handled by the following MsgMain task.

The MsgMain deals with the state transition. The EtherCAT standard defines four major states for the coordination of the master and slave applications at start up and during operation: the init, pre-operational, safe-operational, and operation states [6]. In response to a state change request that is initiated by the master, the MsgMain executes the corresponding operations and acknowledges the request. Note that the real-time process data input and ouput can only be fully functional in the operation state. The MsgMain also handles the non-real-time data transfer. Considering the role of the MsgMain, we run it in background with the lowest priority. It means that it does not have a period and executes in a best effort style whenever the CPU is available after running all the higher priority tasks.

div.head: C. CANopen and CiA 402 for Standardized Drive Interface
div.p: We have adopted the CANopen [2] and CiA 402 profile [3] for the application layer protocol. The CANopen is a widelyused high level communication standard defined by the CAN in Automation (CiA) organization. The adoption of CANopen greatly enhances the interoperability of the motor drive and makes its interface independent of the underlying physical layer, i.e., the EtherCAT.

The CANopen differentiates Process Data Objects (PDOs) and Service Data Objects (SDOs). PDOs are trasmitted in a fast and efficient way and are mainly used for cyclic real-time process data while SDOs are for accessing the configuration and control parameters of the slave devices. In our implementation, PDOs and SDOs are respectively handled by the MsgInt and MsgMain tasks.

The CiA 402 profile specifies the PDOs and SDOs for the control of eletrical drives. The modes of operation that is defined by the CiA402 can be classified into three cyclic synchronous modes (position, velocity, and torque) and a number of profile-based modes. Depending on the mode of operation, the CiA 402 describes a number of mandatory and optional objects. Without loss of generality, we only deal with the implementation and analysis of those cyclic modes.

div.head: IV. ANALYSIS AND PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: This section evaluates the performance of the developed networked drive. We analyze the end-to-end delay for the control command and discuss the responsiveness and achievable throughput for non-real-time traffic in respect of the command mode.

div.head: A. Drive-Local Delay for Host Command
div.p: As one of the essential performance metrics of the drive, we analyze the drive-local command delay, i.e., the time interval from the arrival of a host command at the drive to the actuation of the associated motor. The command delay D drive is calculated as:
div.formula: D drive = R MsgInt + T MotorAct + R MotorAct , (1
div.p: where R τ and T τ refer to the worst-case response time and the period of task τ , respectively. Because, in a cyclic mode of operation, the MsgInt task is cyclically activated by the host command, we can think of it as a periodic task. Our measurement results for the task release time confirm this assumption -the ESC interrupt showed a high degree of periodicity with a maximum jitter of a few microseconds. The values of R MsgInt and R MotorAct are calculated for each command mode, i.e., the position, velocity, or torque mode according to a deterministic delay bound analysis called the time demand analysis [13]. This analysis gives us an exact bound on the worst response times of tasks with arbitrary phases, which are scheduled by a fixed-priority scheduling. It computes the worst response time of a lowest priority task assuming a time instant where all higher priority tasks arrive simultaneously.

div.head: B. Calculation of Task Execution Times
div.p: On the developed drive platform, we measured the times for task execution and system overhead. For the control host, we used the Beckhoff TwinCAT operating on Windows XP. For measurement, probe codes have been inserted to read the timer counter register. The frequency of the timer was set to 30 MHz, meaning that each tick count corresponds to 1/30 us. Table II summarizes the measurement results. As the system overhead, we consider the context switch time because it was found to be non-negligible in the DSP-based drive system. The execution time for a task body refers to the required computation time for each period. According to a classical analysis approach

div.p: for task switch overhead, for periodic tasks, the time for two full-task switches is added to the execution time: one for the schedule in and out of the task itself and the other for possible preemption of a unique lower-priority task [9]. Therefore, in computing the command delay, we took into account both the task body and the task switch times. Note that the MsgMain, a non-periodic task does not have the switch overhead.

As expected, the execution time of MotorAct varied according to the command mode used. It requires the most computing capacity in the position mode. This is because the position control includes the other velocity and torque loops inside.

The MsgInt needs about 15 μs for handling the real-time CANopen objects. According to the CiA 402 profile, we used four mandatory PDOs for cyclic synchronous modes of operations: for example, the ControlWord, StatusWord, TargetPosition, and PositionActual PDOs for position mode. Note that the execution time has been measured when the MsgInt is in the fully functional mode, i.e., the operation enabled mode as specified by the CiA 402 profile. In this mode, the execution time includes the ESC processing and the CANopen handling.

For the MsgMain task, we assume that the drive is in the EtherCAT operation state and does not consider the processing for state transition. The computation time for MsgMain increases in proportion to the volume of non-real-time messages. div.head: C. End-to-End Command Delay
div.p: The end-to-end delay from the release of a control command at the host to motor acutation at drive k can be given as follows:
div.formula: D e2e (k) = D comm (k) + D drive ,(3)
div.p: where D comm (k) is proportional to the value of k due to the line topology of the target system. Fortunately, an accurate analysis of D comm (k) for EtherCAT has already been conducted in [15]. According to the analysis, D comm (k) is expressed as follows:
div.formula: D comm (k) = t host (s) + k × t drive (4
div.p: where t host is the total forwarding time of a message of size s on the host side, which is linearly proportional to the number of EtherCAT packets composing the message of size s, and t drive is the total forwarding time of a message on the drive side, which has a constant of 1 μs, irrespective of the message size. Assuming k = 10 and a payload of 16 bytes per motor drive, D comm (k) is calculated as 25 μs.

Fig. 4. End-to-end delay from host command release to motor acutation Fig. 4 shows the end-to-end delay at the 10-th drive. According to the deterministic delay bound analysis, the R MsgInt , the worst case response time of MsgInt are computed as 79.31, 88.91, 141.97 μs for the torque, velocity, and position mode, respectively. As shown in the figure, the drive has a particularly long end-to-end delay in the position mode. This can be ascribed to the relatively high processor utilization by the MotorAct in the position mode.

div.head: D. Achievable Throughput for Non-Real-Time Traffic
div.p: Figure 5 shows an estimated throughput of the non-real-time traffic according to the master cycle, i.e., the period of the MsgInt task. The throughput has been analytically calculated, considering the cummulative idle time that can be utilized by the MsgMain task and the computation time for handling nonreal-time traffic, for a sufficiently large time interval. Since the worst-case response time of the MsgInt has been analyzed to be slightly less than 150 μs, we only consider periods greater than or equal to 150 μs.

The reason that different motor command modes gives quite different throughput values is again that the utilization of the MotorAct task is quite different according to the command mode: 48.5% for the torque mode, 58.1% for the velocity mode, and 74.1% for the position mode. Thus, in the position mode, we have a very low percentage of idle CPU times Fig. 5. Throughput of non-real-time traffic left for the MsgMain task, and this is why we obtain such a low throughput. This implies that, for the position mode, noticeably improved performance can be expected even with a slightly faster processor. For periods greater than 600 μs, we could observe that the throughputs converge approximately to 2.6, 2.1, and 1.3 MegaByte/Sec, respectively for the torque, velocity, and position modes.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents the implementation and analysis of a networked motor drive equipped with the EtherCAT, an open standard real-time Ethernet. For a precision motion system, we should be able to accurately characterize the performance of motor drives because such a motion system typically involves highly synchronized actuation among its associated motors. In this paper, we describe the implementation of an Ethernetbased motor drive on a priority-based preemptive scheduler. Considering the requirements of the drive hardware, the task decomposition and scheduling parameters have been carefully determined. Then, according to a deterministic delay bound analysis called the time demand analysis, we calculate the worst-case delay taken for the actuation of a host command. Based on a response time analysis and the times measured from the drive testbed, we discuss the end-to-end delay for a control command and the achievable throughput for non-realtime IP traffic. It turned out that the command mode significantly affects both the end-to-end delay and the achievable throughput because the drive software shows quite different processor utilizations according to the command mode.

The detailed description and analysis given in this paper, we believe, is expected to provide useful design guidelines and insight even for other networked motion systems with different processor and industrial Ethernet hardware.
